se-abate-1.explanation: Letting the bidding run because nothing is slowing it needs a word for dying down, and abate and subside both leave the bidding losing force.
se-abate-1.stem: The auctioneer let the bidding run, since there was no sign it would _____ before someone in the room finally reached the reserve.

se-acme-1.explanation: Everything after 1910 falls, so the year is the top of the curve, and acme and pinnacle both name that highest point.
se-acme-1.stem: By 1910 the line had reached the _____ of its prosperity; every set of accounts published after that year showed receipts falling.

se-affable-1.explanation: An evening running two hours long against expectations of severity points to warmth and ease, and affable and genial both leave the host equally friendly.
se-affable-1.stem: Guests who came expecting the famously severe critic found instead a host so _____ that the evening ran two hours past its billing.

se-arcane-1.explanation: Needing a translation for specialists in a neighbouring field means very few can follow it, and arcane and abstruse both leave the notation equally impenetrable.
se-arcane-1.stem: The notation is _____ enough that physicists one subfield away ask for a translation before they will agree to referee the paper.

se-caustic-1.explanation: Regret at having invited the criticism, set against gentle praise, means it stung, and caustic and mordant both leave it equally biting.
se-caustic-1.stem: His praise was gentle and his criticism _____, which is why writers sent him their manuscripts and then regretted having done so.

se-condone-1.explanation: Sitting on evidence for years goes past tolerance into tacit approval, and condone and countenance both leave the regulator accepting the practice.
se-condone-1.stem: A regulator that has held the evidence for three years and still acts on none of it does not merely tolerate the practice; it has come to _____ it.

se-copious-1.explanation: Notes valuable enough to outprice the book are there in quantity, and copious and profuse both leave them equally abundant; perfunctory and laconic say the opposite.
se-copious-1.stem: Her marginal notes were so _____ that the second-hand copy sold for more than the first edition it annotated.

se-disparage-1.explanation: Taking back praise two sentences after giving it is running the work down, and disparage and belittle both leave the compliment withdrawn.
se-disparage-1.stem: He could not praise a rival for long without finding some way, two sentences later, to _____ the very work he had just called impressive.

se-dispassionate-1.explanation: Set against a witness with money on the verdict, the blank wants freedom from stake or feeling, which dispassionate and impartial both give.
se-dispassionate-1.stem: What the inquiry needed was an account that was _____, not a fourth statement from someone with money riding on the verdict.

se-forestall-1.explanation: Publishing early to stop rumours that have not started yet is acting first to head them off, and forestall and avert both keep them from arising.
se-forestall-1.stem: The treasury published the figures a day early to _____ the rumours that a leak, which it knew was coming, would otherwise have started.

se-grovel-1.explanation: Abasing yourself to end the lecture rather than explaining is what grovel and kowtow both describe, and either leaves the staff equally servile.
se-grovel-1.stem: Staff worked out that the quickest way out of his office was to _____, since any attempt to explain the decision only lengthened the lecture.

se-implacable-1.explanation: Refusing every concession without discussion for nine weeks is a refusal to be moved, and implacable and adamant both leave the board equally unyielding.
se-implacable-1.stem: Every concession the union offered was refused without discussion, and the board stayed _____ until the strike reached its ninth week.

se-laudable-1.explanation: Nobody objecting to the aim itself sets it against the execution, so the blank wants praise, which laudable and commendable both supply.
se-laudable-1.stem: The aim was _____ even if the execution was not: nobody objects to feeding children, only to the way the contract was quietly let.

se-panache-1.explanation: Carrying an audience past a visible mistake takes dash rather than care, and panache and verve both leave the performance equally spirited.
se-panache-1.stem: She took the last chorus with such _____ that the audience forgot the orchestra had come in two full bars early.

se-surfeit-1.explanation: Crates given away that would normally be sold by the pound means far too many, and surfeit and glut both leave the market oversupplied.
se-surfeit-1.stem: The season produced such a _____ of tomatoes that growers were giving away crates which in a lean year would have been priced by the pound.

se-tawdry-1.explanation: Plastic chandeliers and gilt paint that fool nobody are cheap display, and tawdry and garish both leave the lobby showy and worthless.
se-tawdry-1.stem: The lobby had been done up in plastic chandeliers and gilt paint, so _____ that nobody who had seen the real thing was fooled for a moment.

se-timorous-1.explanation: Dropping her voice the moment she is challenged is a want of nerve, and timorous and diffident both leave the judge equally unassertive.
se-timorous-1.stem: Even after a decade on the bench she remained _____ in open court, dropping her voice to nothing whenever a barrister pushed back at her.

se-wanton-1.explanation: Trees felled for no reason and at nobody's request is destruction without cause, which wanton and gratuitous both supply.
se-wanton-1.stem: The commission found the felling of the orchard to be _____: the trees stood nowhere near the new road, and no one had asked for them to come down.

tc-ambivalent-1.explanation: One reason to want it and one reason not to is a divided feeling, which ambivalent names; apathetic would mean she felt nothing either way.
tc-ambivalent-1.stem: She was _____ about the promotion: it doubled her salary, and it ended the only part of the job she had ever actually liked.

tc-amorphous-1.explanation: No date, no name and no allegation leaves the complaint without shape to answer, which amorphous says; the other four would give it definite form.
tc-amorphous-1.stem: The complaint was too _____ to answer: it carried no date, no name, and no statement of what the company was supposed to have done.

tc-anachronism-1.explanation: An object appearing forty years before it existed is out of its time, which is precisely what anachronism names.
tc-anachronism-1.stem: The sword hung on the wall of that drawing room is one more _____, since the play is set forty years before anything of the pattern was forged.

tc-brazen-1.explanation: Walking out at noon and waving at the camera is theft without any attempt at concealment, which brazen names; the three hiding words say the opposite.
tc-brazen-1.stem: The theft was _____: two men walked in at noon, carried the painting past the desk, and waved at the camera on their way out.

tc-connoisseur-1.explanation: Placing a wine by village and decade is expert judgement earned over forty years, which connoisseur names; dilettante and tyro deny the expertise.
tc-connoisseur-1.stem: Forty years of tasting had made him a _____ of clarets, able to place a wine within a village and a decade from half a glass.

tc-elucidate-1.explanation: Leaving with the same questions means nothing was made clear, and elucidate is the clarifying the lecture failed to do.
tc-elucidate-1.stem: The second lecture did nothing to _____ the first: the students filed out with exactly the three questions they had walked in carrying.

tc-embellish-1.explanation: Drizzle growing into a blizzard over successive tellings is invented detail added for effect, which embellish names; abridge and curtail would shrink it.
tc-embellish-1.stem: Each retelling let him _____ the story a little further, until a two-mile walk in drizzle had become a night march through a blizzard.

tc-enumerate-1.explanation: Going through failures one after another and reaching eleven is listing them in order, which enumerate names; conflate would run them together.
tc-enumerate-1.stem: Asked for specifics, the auditor began to _____ the failures one after another, and had reached eleven before the chairman stopped her.

tc-espouse-1.explanation: Thirty years of attack reversed into a convert's fervour means the paper now backs the tariff, which espouse says; the others continue the attack.
tc-espouse-1.stem: A paper that had spent thirty years attacking the tariff began, within a month of its sale, to _____ it with all the fervour of a convert.

tc-exacting-1.explanation: A square inch a day under a lens is work that demands enormous care, which exacting names; the other four all describe doing it carelessly.
tc-exacting-1.stem: The restoration was _____ work: a square inch a day, under a lens, with brushes that had been trimmed down to three hairs.

tc-extraneous-1.explanation: The weather and the dog are what the piece is not about, so the cut removed what did not belong, which extraneous names; the rest mean it mattered.
tc-extraneous-1.stem: The editor's first pass cut everything _____ — the weather, the drive up, the two paragraphs about the dog — and the piece was sharper for it.

tc-extrapolate-1.explanation: Stretching one year of data across ten is projecting a trend past what was measured, which extrapolate names and which the guess warning confirms.
tc-extrapolate-1.stem: From four quarters of data the model tries to _____ a decade of demand, which is why anything it says about the later years should be read as a guess.

tc-fledgling-1.explanation: Four aircraft set against forty years of reserves marks the airline as new and untested, which fledgling names; venerable and entrenched say the opposite.
tc-fledgling-1.stem: Four aircraft and a single route leave the carrier too _____ to absorb a fuel shock the way a rival with two hundred planes and forty years of reserves can.

tc-hyperbole-1.explanation: Catastrophe for a September defeat is deliberate overstatement, which hyperbole names, and the note that he meant it literally depends on that reading.
tc-hyperbole-1.stem: To call a two-goal defeat in September a catastrophe is _____, though from the tone of the press conference the manager seemed to mean it literally.

tc-impervious-1.explanation: Reading his own bad reviews aloud for entertainment shows the ridicule no longer touches him, which impervious names; indignant would have him stung.
tc-impervious-1.stem: Thirty years of ridicule had left him _____ to it; he read the worst of the reviews aloud at dinner and laughed at the better lines.

tc-impudent-1.explanation: Asking a new department head who really wrote her thesis is bold disrespect, which impudent names; deferential and decorous would not have silenced the room.
tc-impudent-1.stem: The question was _____ enough to silence the room: he asked the newly appointed head of department who had really written her thesis.

tc-incorrigible-1.explanation: Every attempt at correction failing, and the club giving up, means he cannot be reformed, which incorrigible names; the other four say he could be.
tc-incorrigible-1.stem: Three suspensions, two written contracts and a season of supervised training later, the club finally accepted that he was _____ and let him go.

tc-magnanimous-1.explanation: Praising the team that has just beaten you is generosity towards a rival, which magnanimous names; churlish and vindictive describe the opposite reaction.
tc-magnanimous-1.stem: It was _____ of the losing captain to spend ten minutes of his own press conference praising the side that had just knocked his team out.

tc-myopic-1.explanation: Buying a better year now at the cost of a bigger bill later is shortsighted thinking, which myopic names; the other four would praise the decision.
tc-myopic-1.stem: Cutting the maintenance budget to make this year's figures look better is _____: the bill still arrives, five years out and considerably larger.

tc-nominal-1.explanation: Holding the title while the decisions happen elsewhere is leadership in name only, which nominal says; autocratic and imperious would give him real power.
tc-nominal-1.stem: He remained the _____ head of the firm for another decade, but every decision of any consequence had been taken two floors down since the merger.

tc-oblique-1.explanation: Needing two more questions to find out that she had said no marks the answer as indirect, which oblique names; the rest would have made it plain at once.
tc-oblique-1.stem: Her answer was so _____ that it took the committee two further questions to establish that what she had given them was a refusal.

tc-obtuse-1.explanation: The sentence offers only two readings, wilful or real failure to understand, and obtuse is the slowness both share; the others all mean sharp understanding.
tc-obtuse-1.stem: Either he was being _____ on purpose, or he genuinely could not see why turning up two hours late to his own hearing might count against him.

tc-peruse-1.explanation: Reading line by line instead of trusting a summary is careful study, which peruse names; ratify would be signing it and expedite would be hurrying it.
tc-peruse-1.stem: She asked for an hour to _____ the contract line by line rather than sign it on the strength of the summary she had been handed at the door.

tc-pious-1.explanation: Preaching sacrifice while taking three bonuses is moralising he does not live by, the sanctimonious sense of pious; candid would make the talk honest.
tc-pious-1.stem: For all his _____ talk about restraint and shared sacrifice, he had taken three bonuses in a year the fund lost money for everyone else in it.

tc-rhetoric-1.explanation: Grand talk of destiny and sacrifice that adds nothing to a budget request is persuasive language covering little, which rhetoric names.
tc-rhetoric-1.stem: Stripped of the _____ about destiny and sacrifice, the proposal amounts to a request for a larger budget and two more staff.

tc-salubrious-1.explanation: Air prescribed by doctors against city smoke is air that restores health, which salubrious means; fetid and noxious would make the patients worse.
tc-salubrious-1.stem: Doctors sent their patients to the coast for its _____ air, on the theory that sea wind did what the smoke of the city could not.

tc-solicitous-1.explanation: Checking twice an hour on someone who wants nothing is anxious attention, which solicitous names; the other four would stop her asking at all.
tc-solicitous-1.stem: The nurse was so _____ that she checked twice an hour whether the visitor, who had come in only to drop off a form, needed anything at all.

tc-sybarite-1.explanation: Silk sheets, a cook for one dish and wine bought past his means is a life given over to luxury, which is what a sybarite pursues; a miser would spend nothing.
tc-sybarite-1.stem: He lived as a _____: silk sheets, a cook kept on for one dish alone, and a standing order with the wine merchant that outlasted his income.

tc-turpitude-1.explanation: A ground for dismissal that an auditor's report brings into play is serious wickedness, which turpitude names; equanimity and forbearance would be no grounds at all.
tc-turpitude-1.stem: The clause permits dismissal for moral _____, a phrase the trustees had never once had to define until the auditor's report landed.

tc-umbrage-1.explanation: A tone read as rude when brevity was all that was meant causes offence, which umbrage names; levity and accord would mean it was taken well.
tc-umbrage-1.stem: The letter's clipped tone gave _____ where none had been intended; the writer had been in a hurry and meant only to be brief.

tc-veracity-1.explanation: The sentence grants that the man is honest and doubts only what he could see, so what is unimpugned is his truthfulness, which veracity names.
tc-veracity-1.stem: Nothing in the file impugned the _____ of the witness; the difficulty was that an honest man asleep in the next room still could not have seen the car.

tc-veritable-1.explanation: Eight feet of bramble makes the word jungle no exaggeration, and veritable is the intensifier that says the description holds literally.
tc-veritable-1.stem: The brochure's garden proved to be jungle, and _____ jungle at that: eight feet of bramble, and a path that gave out after four yards.
